recipe.history:
Mushrooms occupy a singular position in the culinary history of nearly every food culture on earth — they are neither plant nor animal, a kingdom unto themselves, harvested from forests and fields with reverence and ritual for as long as humans have eaten. Cremini mushrooms, also known as baby bella or brown mushrooms, are a cultivated variety of Agaricus bisporus, the same species as the common white button mushroom but harvested at a slightly older stage when the caps have browned and the flavor has deepened into something earthier and more assertive. Shiitake mushrooms, Lentinula edodes, originated in East Asia — particularly China and Japan — where they have been cultivated on hardwood logs for over a thousand years. The name derives from the Japanese shii tree (a type of oak) and take, meaning mushroom. In Chinese medicine, shiitake were valued not only as food but as medicine, believed to support longevity and boost immune function. By the Song Dynasty (960–1279 CE), shiitake cultivation was a documented agricultural practice in China; in Japan, they became a cornerstone of Buddhist vegetarian cuisine, their meaty umami making them a satisfying substitute for animal protein in temple cooking.

Mushrooms entered American burger culture through two distinct channels: the steakhouse and the vegetarian movement. In steakhouses of the 1960s and 1970s, sautéed mushrooms — typically white buttons cooked in butter with garlic and sherry — were a classic topping for the beef patty, their earthy savory notes deepening the Maillard-crusted beef beneath them. Shiitake and cremini arrived later, carried into mainstream American kitchens in the 1980s and 1990s on the wave of interest in Asian ingredients and artisan produce that followed the rise of the American farmers' market movement and the growing influence of chefs like Nobu Matsuhisa and David Chang. Burger chefs discovered that a blend of cremini and shiitake — the former providing body and moisture, the latter adding a distinctive woodsy, umami-rich depth — created a topping of extraordinary complexity, one that seemed to amplify the beefiness of the patty rather than compete with it. The name of this burger — a riff on 'The Room Where It Happens' from the musical Hamilton — suggests that the mushroom is the seat of power, and in this recipe, it absolutely is.

I became a mushroom-on-burger convert on a rainy Tuesday in November when I had a pound of shiitakes and a half-pound of creminis that needed to be dealt with before they turned. I sliced everything thick, got my cast iron screaming hot with a knob of butter and a splash of olive oil, and threw them all in without crowding — working in batches the way you're supposed to but so rarely do. The sound was tremendous: a roar of steam and fat. I seasoned them aggressively with salt, a little thyme, a splash of dry sherry that I happened to have open, and watched them reduce from a mountain of raw fungi into a glistening, dark, caramelized mound of pure umami. I piled them on a medium-rare patty with a slice of Gruyère and ate it at the kitchen table in my coat because I hadn't even taken it off yet. It was that urgent. That good. That is the meal I think about when I think about why mushrooms deserve top billing.

The philosophy of medium-rare cookery for a beef burger is rooted in a simple truth: temperature is flavor. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the interior of a beef patty is still pink, still juicy, still alive with the complex mineral and fatty flavors that made you choose 80/20 ground chuck in the first place. The sautéed mushroom blend — already rich with glutamates and their own fatty depth from the butter — needs a patty that has retained its own character to meet it as an equal. A well-done patty would be overwhelmed, rendered a mere vehicle for the topping. At medium rare, the beef pushes back, and the result is a genuine conversation between two serious ingredients, conducted at precisely the right temperature.
ingredients: 225g cremini mushrooms, cleaned and sliced 1/4 inch thick
225g shiitake mushrooms, stems removed, caps sliced 1/4 inch thick
60ml dry sherry or dry white wine
kosher salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes until smooth. Rise in an oiled bowl 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly, proof on parchment 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on rack.
2. Prepare the garlic-herb mayo: Combine mayonnaise, grated garlic, parsley, and lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate.

3. Cook the mushroom blend: Heat a large skillet over high heat. Add butter and olive oil. When butter foams and subsides, add cremini mushrooms in a single layer — work in batches if needed; do not crowd. Cook undisturbed for 2–3 minutes until deeply browned on the bottom. Stir and cook 2 more minutes.
4. Add shiitake mushrooms to the skillet. Stir to combine. Cook 3–4 minutes until shiitakes are tender and starting to brown. Add minced garlic and thyme; cook 60 seconds, stirring constantly.

5. Deglaze with dry sherry, scraping up any browned bits. Add soy sauce and balsamic vinegar. Stir and cook until the liquid is almost fully absorbed and the mushrooms look glossy and deeply caramelized, about 2 minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat and keep warm.

6. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and pepper just before cooking.

7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Lay a slice of Gruyère on each patty. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes off heat.
8. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread garlic-herb mayo on both bun halves. Place the Gruyère-topped patty on the bottom bun. Pile a generous heap of the cremini-shiitake mushroom blend on top of the patty. Add butter lettuce, tomato slices, and raw onion. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately.
